why: Politicians are nodes and each hate pair is a directed edge, so the question is simply 'does this directed graph have a cycle?'. Kahn's topological sort answers it: if some nodes can never reach in-degree 0, they sit on a cycle.
hints: Ignore the politics: draw each [u, v] as an arrow u -> v. A cycle means you can follow arrows and come back to where you started.
A directed graph has no cycle exactly when it has a topological order. Repeatedly remove nodes with in-degree 0; if you remove all n, there is no cycle.
Build adjacency lists and in-degree counts, run a queue-based Kahn's algorithm and count removed nodes; answer is removed < n. O(n + E) time and space (or DFS with white/grey/black colouring).
pitfalls: An undirected 'visited' check is wrong here: 0->2 and 1->2 reach node 2 twice without any cycle. Only a back edge to a node still on the current DFS path counts.
A self-loop [u, u] is a cycle of length one.
Politicians with no relationships still count toward n; the graph can be disconnected, so start from every node.
constraints:
• 1 <= n (not stated in the source; assume up to about 10^5)
  • 0 <= u, v < n for every pair [u, v] in hatePairs
  • hatePairs may be empty and may contain self-loops; numeric bounds are not stated in the source
